issues.legal_issue: A tenant who raises a genuine factual dispute about the landlord-tenant relationship and the basis on which possession was obtained must not be denied leave to contest a summary eviction application on the mistaken premise that the relationship was admitted.
material_facts: The tenant sought leave to contest an eviction application and stated that possession had been obtained under an agreement to sell, not as a tenant.
The tenant disputed that a landlord-tenant relationship existed and denied that the alleged tenancy was genuine.
The Rent Controller treated the tenant’s pleadings as admitting the landlord-tenant relationship and refused leave to contest.
The High Court dismissed the revision without addressing that alleged error.
issues.conclusion: The tenant had raised a triable dispute, so refusing leave to contest was unsustainable. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the orders refusing leave and granting eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 14(1)(e) and 25B(1), (4), (6), (8) and (10) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenant served in a qualifying bona fide-requirement eviction proceeding must seek leave to contest by affidavit. Because refusal results in the landlord’s allegations being deemed admitted, the special procedure requires strict interpretation. On a reasonable and purposeful interpretation, leave must not be refused where the tenant’s application and affidavit disclose a triable case. The Court cited no earlier cases.

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_request: A tenant sought permission to contest an eviction application handled through a summary procedure.
predicates.tenant_denied_landlord_tenant_relationsh: The tenant stated that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the parties.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeking to contest a summary eviction application denies the landlord-tenant relationship and says possession arose from an agreement to sell, refusing leave to contest is unsustainable.
